# Final Summary
Russia, South Korea, Pakistan, the Netherlands, Japan, the Czech Republic, and Mexico each maintain distinct education systems shaped by historical, cultural, and socioeconomic factors. Russia emphasizes national cohesion through standardized curricula, mandatory patriotic education, and linguistic integration, with a growing Bologna-aligned higher education model and strong regional language preservation. South Korea prioritizes academic excellence and university access, though student well-being and vocational stigma remain pressing concerns. Pakistan faces deep-rooted gender disparities, underfunding, and quality issues, with literacy improving slowly despite efforts to expand access and inclusion. The Netherlands offers a flexible, student-centered secondary system with strong vocational and academic pathways, supported by quality assurance and inclusive practices, though early tracking and equity gaps persist. Japan maintains rigorous academic standards and high completion rates, supported by strong institutional frameworks and inclusive policies, though excessive exam pressure and mental health challenges remain. The Czech Republic exemplifies institutional stability and academic tradition, with a clear pathway from primary to tertiary education and strong support for students with special needs.
Mexico’s education system has evolved from a state-driven, ideologically charged model in the 1920s–1940s to a more decentralized, secular, and expansive system. Under Lázaro Cárdenas, socialist education promoted anti-religious and collectivist values, triggering resistance from Catholic groups; subsequent reforms under Manuel Avila Camacho and Jaime Torres Bodet shifted toward secular, nationalist curricula and improved teacher training. The 1940s–1960s saw economic growth and expanded access, though rural disparities and illiteracy persisted. Student activism in 1968 and 1971 exposed systemic failures, leading to reforms in adult education and media outreach. The 1990s introduced neoliberal reforms, including decentralization and merit-based teacher pay, amid tensions with the SNTE union. School attendance surged from 3 million in 1950 to 32 million in 2011, and literacy reached 94.86% by 2018. Today, Mexico emphasizes inclusive education, vocational pathways, and access for marginalized groups—including indigenous populations—through initiatives like Intercultural Universities. Despite progress, regional disparities, low secondary completion rates (45%), and weaknesses in teacher training and infrastructure continue to hinder equitable outcomes. The country’s top universities, including UNAM and private institutions like IPADE and EGADE, are internationally recognized, reflecting its growing academic stature.
Canada features a decentralized education system, with provinces holding primary responsibility and the federal government overseeing Indigenous education, military colleges, and funding. Compulsory education begins at age 5–7 and ends at age 16–18, with secondary education typically concluding at Grade 12, except in Quebec, where it ends at Grade 11 (Secondary V), and Grade 13/OAC was phased out in Ontario in 2003. Students may extend study beyond Grade 12 for academic or personal reasons, with Ontario introducing a 34-credit threshold to limit duration. Kindergarten is offered in all provinces, with two-year programs in several regions. Post-secondary education includes universities (offering bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees) and vocational institutions (offering diplomas, certificates, and applied degrees). Admission to universities is competitive, requiring strong academic records—often with GPA cut-offs of 80–90%—and emphasizing extracurricular achievements. Provincial governments primarily fund post-secondary education, with no national accreditation body; degrees are granted via provincial legislation. Canada spends approximately 5.2% of GDP on education, with 51% of Canadians holding tertiary qualifications in 2010—the highest globally—reflecting the growing essentiality of post-secondary education in the labor market. Indigenous studies, antiracism, and cultural programming are increasingly integrated, though access remains limited by geography. Rising tuition fees—particularly in Alberta, where fees increased by 5.7%—have sparked concern, with a new fast-track immigration pathway introduced for foreign students and graduates with Canadian work experience. Education outcomes are shared internationally via the Canadian Education Statistics Council (CESC) and OECD through PCEIP and PISA, enabling comparative analysis and policy refinement.
Canadian education varies significantly by province, with distinct grade structures and terminology. For example, British Columbia uses middle schools (K–7 or 8) and junior secondary schools, while Ontario employs Maternelle and Jardin for early grades; Quebec blends secondary and post-secondary education. Some regions, such as Yellowknife and Saskatchewan, have unique grade groupings or graduation requirements. Each province operates under its own education ministry or department, reflecting the decentralized nature of the system.
New Zealand has a national, free, compulsory, and secular education system established in 1878, rooted in Māori wānanga traditions that were later supplemented by European-style missionary schools. Early childhood education includes licensed centre-based and parent-led services such as Kindergarten, Kohanga Reo, and Playcentre, all regulated by the Ministry of Education and guided by the early learning framework Te Whāriki. Primary education spans Years 1–8, with Years 7–8 as intermediate, followed by secondary education (Years 9–13). Schooling is compulsory from age 6 to 16, with students often staying until age 17. Home schooling requires formal approval, and students with special needs may attend specialist schools until age 21. The system includes state, state-integrated, and private schools, all following national curricula (NZC or Te Marautanga o Aotearoa), with compulsory subjects until Year 10. Students typically progress from primary (Years 1–8) to secondary (Years 9–13), with various school types based on structure, funding, and function: state schools are free and secular, state-integrated schools retain special character (e.g., religious) and charge attendance dues, while private schools rely on tuition. Enrolment schemes, which prioritize local students and use lotteries when full, exist in high-density urban areas. Home schooling and charter schools (now converted to state-integrated) are limited. Around 85% of students attend state schools, with 10% in state-integrated and 4% in private schools.
New Zealand’s zone-based enrolment system, while ensuring equitable access, has drawn criticism for limiting parental choice and reinforcing socio-economic disparities due to inflated property values near high-performing schools. To combat address fraud, schools now require verifiable residency proof, such as statutory declarations. Historically, Māori language education was suppressed, leading to a significant decline in proficiency; however, since the 1980s, revitalization efforts—including kōhanga reo, kura kaupapa Māori schools, the Māori Language Act (1987), and Treaty of Waitangi recognition—have strengthened Māori-medium education. Today, Māori language is taught in both immersion and English-medium settings, though enrolment has slightly declined. Māori students in kura kaupapa achieve significantly higher NCEA Level 3 pass rates (58%) compared to mainstream schools (35%). The school year runs from late January to mid-December, divided into four ten-week terms with breaks in between.
Teaching quality and a culture prioritizing children’s learning are key to success in New Zealand’s education system, though it lags behind Hong Kong, Japan, and Singapore in performance. Strong parental involvement is present, yet Māori and Pacific Island students underperform Pākehā students in academic achievement—ranking 34th and 44th, respectively, in PISA. Bullying is widespread, with New Zealand having the second-highest bullying rates globally. The Ombudsman’s 2009 report called for mandatory anti-bullying programs, but government initiatives such as the $60 million "Positive Behaviour for Learning" plan have yielded limited results. Schools lack a unified anti-bullying policy, resulting in inconsistent responses across institutions.
Bangladesh operates a multi-sectoral education system comprising primary, secondary, tertiary, technical/vocational, and alternative education. The system is structured into clear stages—pre-primary (Nursery to KG), primary (Grades I–V), secondary (Grades VI–X), and higher secondary (Grades XI–XII)—with specialized boards such as Qawmi (Islamic-based) and Alia (non-Islamic) providing alternative curricula. Vocational, diploma, and degree programs are available across levels, culminating in postgraduate and doctoral studies. The national curriculum offers three streams—Arts, Commerce, and Science—after Class 9, with limited subject choice. Exams (JSC, SSC, HSC) are standardized and do not include classroom performance. Schools include international (e.g., English or French-medium), religiously affiliated, and national curriculum institutions. Cadet colleges—military-run, disciplined institutions—are prominent. The government plans to build 1,000 primary schools in underserved areas. Tertiary education includes 43 public, 103 private, 2 international, and specialized universities, regulated by the University Grants Commission. Public universities are government-subsidized and competitive in admissions; private universities offer greater flexibility, attract foreign students, and are self-funded. Private medical colleges are affiliated with public universities. Technical and vocational education is administered by the Technical Education Board and Directorate of Technical Education (DTE), offering diplomas leading to bachelor’s degrees through Polytechnic Institutes. Alternative education includes international schools (offering English-medium curricula such as Cambridge, Edexcel, and IB) and the Madrasah system, which focuses on Islamic studies in Arabic, Bengali, or English and often serves marginalized communities. The system emphasizes national standards and access to international pathways, with ongoing reforms in assessment and equity. The discontinuation of the PEC and JSC exams in 2023 reflects a shift toward more streamlined and modernized assessment practices.
Bangladesh’s education system includes a dual madrasah structure—Qawmi (private, small enrollment) and Alia (government-subsidized, larger enrollment), with Alia offering Arabic alongside general education. Refugee education, particularly for Rohingya children, remains a persistent challenge due to limited access to formal schooling, though UNICEF and government initiatives are expanding opportunities. Non-formal education, primarily delivered by NGOs like BRAC, serves dropouts and vulnerable populations, with graduates often re-entering mainstream schools. A standardized grading system uses a 33% pass mark, incorporating GPA and letter grades, with optional subjects allowing additional grade points. Religious education is part of the national curriculum for Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Christianity, though non-Muslim students often study religion independently. Despite progress in access and free curriculum distribution, key challenges persist, including outdated curricula, overreliance on rote learning, lack of industry-oriented education, and insufficient support for marginalized groups. Bangladesh faces ongoing challenges in teacher quality, with 15.5% absenteeism, gender disparities in rural areas, low school attendance, high dropout and repetition rates, and rising education costs. Public education spending ranges from 0.94% to 2.2% of GDP, reflecting limited investment relative to the scale of the system. The literacy rate has improved significantly, rising from 51.77% in 2011 to 74.66% in 2022.
Saudi Arabia features a free, Islamic-rooted education system, with strong religious instruction—23 periods per week in sciences versus 9 in primary—oversight by the Ministry of Education. Primary education is compulsory (6 years), with English introduced from Grade 1. Secondary education includes general and technical tracks, and Islamic studies were consolidated into one subject in 2021. The system enjoys high enrollment rates (95.9% in primary, 91.8% in secondary in 2007) and strong government investment (5.1% of GDP in 2006). While challenges remain in teacher quality and access, Saudi Arabia’s system is more structured, religiously grounded, and well-funded compared to Bangladesh’s, reflecting a stronger institutional framework and long-term national investment in education. Since the establishment of its first university in 1957, Saudi Arabia has significantly expanded its higher education system, with 24 government universities and private institutions offering bachelor’s, master’s, and PhD programs. The system emphasizes humanities and social sciences (over 70% of students), with women now constituting 60% of university students—surpassing men in undergraduate enrollment by 2015—and achieving legal practice rights. The Kingdom offers one of the world’s largest scholarship programs for women, including doctorates abroad, and Princess Nora bint Abdul Rahman University is the largest women-only university. Gifted education began in 1969 with policy frameworks and has evolved through enrichment programs like the Summer Enrichment Program (SEP), supported by Mawhiba, focusing on STEM and creativity.
Saudi Arabia's education system is characterized by a strong emphasis on religious instruction, particularly Quranic memorization and Islamic doctrine, which has drawn criticism for promoting intolerance, rote learning, and stifling innovation and entrepreneurship. While literacy rates are relatively high—85% for adults and 98.1% for youth—significant regional disparities and gender gaps persist, with the lowest illiteracy rates in Riyadh and the highest in Jizan. The King Abdullah Project and the Tatweer reform program aim to modernize education by training over 400,000 teachers, promoting extracurricular activities, and shifting toward problem-solving and vocational training. Despite efforts to remove anti-Semitic and intolerant content from textbooks, some controversial teachings remain. International schools, including British and Philippine institutions, serve expatriate communities, reflecting the country’s diverse population. Critics argue that the system must evolve to meet global economic demands through greater emphasis on English language proficiency and secular, market-ready skills.
